initial_assessment: 34-year-old man, performance status 2, no comorbidities, presenting with one week of headache and vomiting. MRI shows a well-circumscribed, lobulated, extra-axial/cortically based left frontal mass (4.2 x 3.5 x 3.0 cm) and a separate 5 mm intensely and uniformly enhancing nodule on the posterior pial surface at C6 with normal cord caliber. Stereotactic biopsy is reported as 'suggestive of' an intracranial mesenchymal tumor with spinal drop metastasis. The diagnosis is therefore provisional: the category 'mesenchymal' is established only at the morphologic level, and the specific entity, grade, and molecular class are NOT established in the source. Working assumption for planning only: a CNS mesenchymal neoplasm of uncertain grade with possible neuraxial (CSF) dissemination, treated as high-risk until proven otherwise. The spinal nodule has not been reported as sampled; it is presumed to be the same tumor, which is an assumption that must be confirmed. Differential diagnosis to be resolved by pathology and molecular testing: (1) solitary fibrous tumor/hemangiopericytoma (CNS WHO 2021 grade 2 or 3; NAB2-STAT6 fusion; the most common CNS mesenchymal entity with an extra-axial, intensely enhancing appearance and a propensity for CSF spread); (2) round-cell or Ewing-like sarcoma with CIC-DUX4 or other EWSR1/FUS-non-ETS fusions; (3) other sarcomas such as rhabdomyosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, or undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma; (4) meningioma with sarcomatous or dedifferentiated change; (5) melanoma, which must be excluded because intense enhancement and leptomeningeal spread are typical and it changes management entirely; (6) primary CNS lymphoma and carcinoma metastasis are less likely given the mesenchymal morphology but are not excluded by the report. The management-relevant unknowns are the entity, the grade, whether the lesion is melanocytic, sarcomatous, or meningeal in origin, whether the spinal nodule is the same tumor, and whether the frontal mass is resectable without unacceptable deficit.
diagnostic_confirmation_and_staging: Diagnostic confirmation: (a) neuropathology re-review of the existing stereotactic biopsy at a neuro-oncology reference center, with a full histologic report (cellularity, mitoses per 10 HPF, necrosis, vascular pattern, pleomorphism, growth pattern); (b) immunohistochemistry panel including STAT6, CD34, BCL2, EMA, SSTR2, S100, SOX10, HMB45, Melan-A, desmin, myogenin, MyoD1, smooth muscle actin, h-caldesmon, pan-cytokeratin, SMARCB1/INI1, BRG1, CD99, FLI1, NKX2-2, WT1, ERG, TLE1, GFAP, OLIG2, and H3K27me3 as indicated; (c) molecular testing: DNA methylation profiling (the most useful adjunct where IHC is equivocal in CNS mesenchymal tumors), RNA-based fusion sequencing (NAB2-STAT6, CIC-DUX4, EWSR1 and FUS fusions, other round-cell sarcoma fusions), and targeted DNA sequencing including CDKN2A/B, TP53, NF2, PTEN, and TERT promoter, plus BRAF, NRAS, and KIT if melanoma remains possible. If the biopsy material is insufficient for these tests, that is an indication for open resection rather than repeat needle sampling (see plan). Spinal nodule: confirm whether it was sampled; sample only if the result would change management and can be done safely, which is to be decided at the tumor board. Staging: (1) gadolinium-enhanced MRI of the entire neuraxis, meaning brain plus full spine (cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral) with thin sections, to define all drop lesions, leptomeningeal enhancement, dural tail, bone or sinus involvement, edema, and hydrocephalus; (2) systemic staging with contrast CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis, or FDG PET/CT, to look for an extracranial primary or metastases, plus skin, lymph node, and testicular examination; (3) CSF cytology only after neurosurgery confirms no obstructive hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure and the lumbar approach is considered safe with the known C6 lesion; this is staging information, not an immediate requirement; (4) baseline laboratory tests: CBC, comprehensive metabolic panel, coagulation studies, LDH, type and screen, and HIV and hepatitis serology before any surgery or systemic therapy; (5) functional mapping for the left frontal lesion (fMRI and/or diffusion tractography for language and motor cortex) before any resection.
immediate_management_plan: Short-horizon plan only. No chemotherapy or definitive radiotherapy regimen is proposed, because the entity, grade, extent, and resectability are not established and no treatable entity has been identified. Steps: (1) Urgent neurosurgery review within days, given a symptomatic 4 cm mass with headache and vomiting. Decide with neuropathology and neuro-oncology whether open resection is preferred over the existing biopsy, both for mass effect and to obtain adequate tissue for molecular diagnosis; extent of resection is limited by eloquent cortex identified in step (5) of the staging section. (2) Corticosteroids: if peritumoral edema is causing symptoms, use dexamethasone at a standard dose with taper, gastroprotection, and glucose monitoring, per local protocol. Because primary CNS lymphoma remains in the differential and steroids can obscure its histology, check with neuropathology before starting unless symptoms are severe. (3) Symptomatic care: antiemetic (for example ondansetron), electrolyte monitoring, and avoidance of sedatives that confound neurological assessment. (4) Seizures: none are reported, so routine antiseizure prophylaxis is not recommended; if seizures occur, start levetiracetam and involve neurology and neurosurgery. (5) Neurological surveillance: document a baseline examination including visual fields, fundoscopy for papilledema, cranial nerves, motor and sensory function, gait, and a spinal cord level examination for myelopathy. Urgent MRI and neurosurgical review are required for any new deficit, declining consciousness, papilledema, worsening headache or vomiting, or new myelopathy, since these can indicate herniation or cord compression. (6) Spinal lesion: no cord compression is reported, so no spinal intervention is indicated now unless there is neurological deterioration; spinal surgery or radiotherapy is not indicated until the diagnosis is established. (7) Supportive care: functional assessment with physiotherapy and occupational therapy given performance status 2, driving restriction per local law, and social work and psychological support. Discuss fertility preservation (sperm banking) before any therapy that may be gonadotoxic. (8) Multidisciplinary review: present at a neuro-oncology and sarcoma tumor board including neurosurgery, neuropathology, neuroradiology, radiation oncology, and medical oncology, with the patient involved in discussions. Re-review when pathology and molecular results are available, with the timing set by laboratory turnaround. (9) Entity-triggered pathways, not to be started now: SFT/hemangiopericytoma with NAB2-STAT6 fusion leads to the SFT/HPC pathway; sarcoma fusion or rhabdomyosarcoma leads to sarcoma or adolescent-and-young-adult referral; melanoma leads to melanoma evaluation with BRAF/NRAS/KIT results; meningioma leads to the grade-based meningioma pathway; lymphoma leads to hematology referral; carcinoma leads to a primary-site search. Disease-directed options and sequencing should be decided only after these results are available.
missing_information: Final histologic diagnosis under CNS WHO 2021, including grade, with mitotic count per 10 HPF, necrosis, and cellularity.
Full immunohistochemistry results (including STAT6, CD34, SOX10, S100, desmin, myogenin, INI1, and others) and whether the biopsy material is adequate for further testing.
Molecular results: DNA methylation class, RNA fusion findings (NAB2-STAT6, CIC-DUX4, EWSR1 or FUS fusions), and targeted DNA sequencing.
Whether the C6 spinal nodule was sampled or only imaged, and its histology if sampled.
Full-neuraxis contrast MRI details: thoracic, lumbar, and sacral drop lesions, leptomeningeal enhancement, dural tail, bone or sinus involvement, peritumoral edema, midline shift, and hydrocephalus.
Systemic staging results (CT or PET), extracranial primary search, and skin, lymph node, and testicular examination findings.
Detailed neurological examination: focal deficits, seizure history, visual fields, papilledema, language dominance, motor function, and cord-level signs.
Baseline laboratory values: CBC, metabolic panel, LDH, coagulation studies, HIV and hepatitis serology.
Resectability assessment: relationship of the frontal mass to eloquent cortex, functional MRI or tractography results, and neurosurgical opinion.
CSF cytology status, intracranial pressure assessment, and whether a lumbar puncture is considered safe.
Performance status detail beyond the reported value of 2, social support, patient goals and preferences, and fertility wishes.
